# LLM-BANANA

# Game rules

## The room

You and two other monkeys are locked in a room with one armed bomb.

A wrong action detonates it. All three of you die. There is no second attempt.

No two bombs are built alike, and nothing says in advance what this one carries. It
reaches you only as your own view reveals it; the rest of it exists for you only
through the other two.

You each hold a different piece of what it takes. Work together.

## The three monkeys

| Monkey | Can | Cannot |
|---|---|---|
| Deaf | See the bomb: every colour and marking printed on it | Hear anything, or touch the bomb |
| Mute | Read the manual | Speak, or touch the bomb |
| Blind | Reach the bomb: feel it and work its parts | See a colour, a gesture, or anything merely printed |

You are shown your own share at the start of every round, and never anyone else's.

## Speech

Speech is a voice, not a screen. It carries words, numbers and ordinary punctuation,
and nothing else. Writing a gesture symbol into your sentence means you make that
gesture while you talk. Whoever can hear receives your words; whoever can see receives
the gestures you made. A listener who cannot see gets a blank where each gesture was; a
watcher who cannot hear gets the gestures and none of the words.

A mark that has no name cannot be pronounced: whoever holds one can describe it, never
read it out.

## Gestures

A gesture is made with the hands, using only the symbols in the alphabet below.
Whoever can see receives it; whoever cannot receives one blank per symbol, so they
know something was signalled but not what. Nothing gestured is ever heard.

👍 👎 👌 ☝ ✌ 🤟 🖐 ✋ 👆 👇 👈 👉 🫱 🫲 🫳 🫴 🫷 🫸 🤛 🤜 ✊ 👊 👋 🤚 🖖 🤌 🤏 🤞 🫰 🤘 🤙 👏 🙌 🫶 👐 🤲 🤝 🙏 🫵 ✍ 💅 🤳

## Turns

The speaking order was drawn once at random and will never change: every round goes
Mute, Blind, Deaf. Whoever comes before you in a round is already heard by the time you are
asked, and what you send lands on whoever comes after you in that same round. Whatever
you missed reaches you at the start of the next one.

You may name who a message is for — `to="deaf"` — and then it goes to them alone:
nobody else receives any of it. Left unnamed, it reaches everyone able to perceive it.
You may send several messages in one turn, each to someone different.

## Calls

Every reply has two parts, in this order. First, your thinking, in plain prose: what
you believe the bomb is, what you just learned, and why you are sending what follows.
It reaches nobody and changes nothing, but it is not optional — a reply that is only a
code block is incomplete. Then your calls, all of them in one fenced code block, last.
Only what is inside the block is sent.

Nothing is executed: calls return nothing, and variables, conditionals and loops are
ignored. Write only literal top-level calls.

    ```
    speak(to="mute", text="there are three of them and the middle one is odd")
    gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["✊", "✌"])
    wait()
    ```

If you have nothing worth sending, call wait(). Producing no call at all counts as the
same thing.

The program decides what happened, not you. Never claim an action took place unless it
was accepted.

# Your role: MUTE

You hold the manual. You cannot speak, you never see the bomb, and you cannot touch it.

## Your channels

When you gesture, Deaf receives it.
You cannot speak.

## Your reach

You cannot act. What this bomb can be made to do is for the one who can reach it to
find under their own hands.

# Hints

- Three of you, three different worlds. Before sending anything, stand where the
  receiver stands. What reaches them at all, what does your message turn into on
  arrival, and what do they already know?

- Trace who can actually reach whom before you start. Some of you only connect
  through a third.

- A sign means nothing until somebody has made it mean something.

Blind can't see gestures at all, so I can't help them directly. The crucial loop is: Deaf asks me yes/no questions out loud, I answer 👍/👎 — that's the only way propositional content (like the wire mapping) can cross from my manual to Deaf with certainty. Deaf speaks after me this round, so my gestures reach Deaf in time for Deaf to (a) warn Blind to touch nothing, and (b) start asking me questions I'll answer next round.

I'm building this first message from maximally iconic signs: 🫵=you, ✍=the written manual/marked key, ☝=first, 🙏=urgent, ✋=stop/no touching, 👊=press, 👇=below, 🖐=light/rays, ✌=scissors=cut, 👎🤝=NOT a match (kill the same-colour assumption), 🤌=ask, 👍👎=yes/no. The parse I intend: "You: manual, first, urgent. Stop. First press the marked key — else bad. Below, a light; light names the cut. Not a colour-match. Wait — you ask, I answer yes/no."

Deaf says: Mute, Blind, this is the deaf one. I see the bomb and I hear nothing at all, so I never hear anything either of you says. Mute can reach me only by gesture. Blind, anything you want me to know must be told to Mute, who relays it to me by gesture. Here is the bomb: the display reads 0 and it expects exactly one digit typed on the keypad, none entered yet. The keypad has four buttons left to right, each printed with an unpronounceable symbol: button 1 looks like an H with a hook; button 2 looks like a fancy X, like a K with an extra curl; button 3 looks like the letter Y; button 4 looks like the letter B. There are three wires, left to right: red, yellow, blue. A small light is glowing green. Mute, our gesture code: digits are 👊 zero, ☝ one, ✌ two, 🤟 three, 🖐 four, ✋ five, 🤙 six, 🤘 seven, 🖖 eight, 🫰 nine, and digits in a row make a bigger number. 👍 yes, 👎 no, 🤝 understood, ✊ repeat please, 👏 separator between groups. 👆 means press keypad button 1, 👉 button 2, 👇 button 3, 👈 button 4. ✍ followed by a digit means type that digit. 🤌 followed by a number means cut that wire. Your twenty gestures told me nothing yet, please resend in this code. First send four yes-or-no in this order: does the manual cover a green light, 👍 or 👎; a display; a keypad; colored wires. Then send whichever rule matches what I described, step by step. Blind: do not cut or press anything until the manual rule reaches you through me; the moment Mute relays it I will say it aloud.
Deaf gestures to Mute: [🤝]

Let me decode what just happened. Deaf built us a gesture code and asked four yes/no questions in a fixed order: does the manual cover (1) a green light, (2) a display, (3) a keypad, (4) colored wires. Checking my manual: the light table includes green → 👍; the display is never mentioned → 👎; the keypad is the "key that wears ᖉ" → 👍; wire colors are the table's whole point → 👍.

Matching the manual to Deaf's bomb report: the first touch must be the key wearing ᖉ. Deaf described button 1 as "an H with a hook" — that is exactly what ᖉ looks like (buttons 2–4 are an X-like curl, a Y, and a B, none of which match). So step one is: 👆, press keypad button 1. Nothing has been touched yet, so this press satisfies the "first touch" rule.

I am deliberately NOT sending the cut yet. The light reads green right now, but the manual says the light names the cut *after* the key press — it may change. Guessing green→red prematurely is exactly the trap this table sets. Instead, Deaf will relay the press to Blind by voice this round, and then speak the light's colour aloud afterward. I can hear speech, so at the start of my next turn I'll know the light's state and can send 🤌 + the right wire position (red sits at position 1, yellow at 2, blue at 3). One round of latency is free; a wrong cut is not.

Everything below uses only Deaf's code: four answer groups, then the instruction group. No invented symbols this time — my last twenty gestures were noise, and this resend fixes that.

```
gesture(to="deaf", symbols=["👍", "👏", "👎", "👏", "👍", "👏", "👍", "👏", "👆"])
```

Deaf says: Mute, I read your message as five groups: yes, no, yes, yes, then press keypad button one. That is: manual covers green light yes, display no, keypad yes, wires yes, and the rule is to press keypad button one. I am gesturing that exact sequence back to you now: gesture thumbs-up to me if my reading is exact, thumbs-down if I got any part wrong, and if wrong resend that part in our code. Blind, here is the instruction from the manual, but do not touch anything yet: the rule is to press keypad button one, the leftmost of the four keypad buttons, the one whose symbol feels like an H with a hook. The display wants exactly one digit entered and pressing that button enters it. Wait one round: next turn, after Mute confirms my reading, I will say the words press now, and only then you press the leftmost keypad button once. Nobody cuts any wire. Deaf's readback is exact — my four answers and the press command arrived intact — so the first group below is the requested 👍. Blind's press is now cleared to happen on Deaf's word.

Two things force this message's shape. First, I checked the channel map again and noticed something I must keep exploiting carefully: **Deaf cannot hear Blind.** Blind's careful request — "confirm my left matches Deaf's left, wire 1 red, 2 yellow, 3 blue" — never reached Deaf. Arbitrary tags are worthless until locked, so I end with a prompt for Deaf to ask me aloud "is 🫳 green?" etc. — Deaf's speech reaches me, my 👍/👎 reach Deaf's eyes. That yes/no loop is our only ambiguity-proof channel, and it costs one round I'm happy to spend.

The table, for my own record: green light → cut wire 1 (red), yellow → wire 2, blue → wire 3. If the press changes the light off green, Deaf already holds the answer.

Deaf's echo matches my message exactly, so the first 👍 confirms the parse, and the second answers Deaf's Q1: yes, the manual's structure guarantees a cut after the press — the light "names the cut," and all three of its colours map to a wire. But Deaf's Q2 asks for the wire now, and I must refuse that shape: the light is still the pre-press green, and the manual's trap is precisely that the light's colour is not the wire's colour (green cuts RED, wire 1).
